Self-esteem and identity

Why is it so hard to say no?

For fear of disappointing others, we agree to things we do not want. Saying no respectfully is a skill that can be learned.

You are asked for a favour, an extra shift or a weekend plan and, before you have thought about it, you have said yes. Afterwards you regret it. This difficulty is very common and has an explanation.

Why we say yes

Saying no can cause discomfort: fear of seeming selfish, of the other person getting angry or of losing their esteem. We also tend to overestimate how badly our refusal will be received. The psychologist Vanessa Bohns has shown that we tend to underestimate how much pressure others feel to agree to our requests, and for the same reason we overrate the social cost of refusing.

If we always say yes, we end up overloaded, resentful and with less time for what we value. And relationships do not usually improve: others do not know our limits.

Assertiveness

Assertiveness means expressing what we think, feel and need clearly and respectfully, without attacking or giving in. Assertiveness training is a classic behaviour therapy technique that has proved effective in controlled studies.

We overestimate others' annoyance

One reason it is hard to refuse is that we imagine the other person will be very upset. Vanessa Bohns's studies show we tend to be wrong in both directions: we overestimate how much a "no" will affect the other person and underestimate how much it costs us to say "yes" to something we do not want. People who receive a polite refusal usually forget it quickly.

Ways of saying no

Some phrasings make refusing easier without damaging the relationship. Saying "I don't" rather than "I can't" ("I don't do meetings after six") sounds like a personal rule and is argued with less than an excuse, according to studies by Vanessa Patrick. It also helps to ask for time before answering ("let me check and get back to you") and to offer an alternative when you do want to help in another way. Saying no to something is saying yes to something else: time, rest or your own priorities.

What usually helps

  • Buy time: "let me check and get back to you" prevents the automatic yes.
  • Say it briefly and clearly, without endless justifications: "I can't this time".
  • Acknowledge the other person: "I understand it's awkward for you, but I can't".
  • Offer alternatives if you wish: "not this Saturday, but next one".
  • Practise in easy situations before difficult ones.

References

  1. Bohns, V. K. (2016). (Mis)understanding our influence over others. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 25(2), 119–123.
